question: What is the meaning of logistics in relation to design and production?
description: In the context of design and production, logistics refers to the planning, implementation, and control of the efficient flow and storage of raw materials, components, and finished products from the point of origin to the point of consumption. This process is crucial for ensuring that materials and products are available when needed, minimizing waste and inefficiencies, and optimizing the overall production process. In the construction industry, effective logistics management can facilitate the reuse and recycling of construction and demolition waste (C&DW), improve the management of building materials, and support the transition towards a circular economy by reducing environmental impacts and costs.

Current practice often disposes of materials at the end of use because it is 
easiest to buy new materials. Reused building materials often face 
additional challenges with supposed costs, liability, and lack of origi-nal 
product information (Farooque et al., 2019). Emerging frameworks and 
research point to the intersection of digi-talization and circular economy 
for the built environment as a means to facilitate development and 
mitigate costs (Çetin et al., 2021).
It is critical, therefore, to address digital traceability in CCSCs, 
focusing on efficient data management for products in construction. To 
track and trace materials in CCSCs involves monitoring the production, 
location, and attributes over time. This research focuses on one aspect of 
this by pro-viding a quantitative analysis of three data carriers (Quick- 
Response (QR) codes, Near-Field Communication (NFC) chips, and 
Direct Product Marking (DPM)) to facilitate the reuse of building com­
ponents after production and use. The work begins with a review of 
relevant literature, moves into the research design, then provides 
exploratory and statistical analysis of the experimental results, and, 
lastly, positions these results as a contribution to research and practice.
2. Background
Existing literature is reviewed on the intersection of circular supply 
chains, product passports and product data, and tracking devices in the 
Internet of Things (IoT).
2.1. Circular construction supply chain
Research in circular economy applications within the Architecture, 
Engineering, and Construction (AEC) industry often conflates reuse with 
the recycling of construction and demolition waste (C&DW) (Ghaffar 
et al., 2020; Ghisellini et al., 2018). However, insights can be gleaned, 
such as the importance of logistics, costs, and operations in facilitating 
the reuse and recycling of C&DW (Ghaffar et al., 2020). The literature 
supports the claim that obstacles to C&DW management include the lack 
of knowledge of materials, the quality of products, and lack of awareness 
of environ-mental costs (Ghisellini et al., 2018). Information on the 
physical, mechanical, and economic attributes are found to be most 
important for the reuse of building materials (Byers et al., 2024c). 
Furthermore, the lack of information sharing between stages of the 
building life cycle also inhibits a successful circular economy 
(Wijewickrama et al., 2021b).
Green supply chains have been significantly studied in the past in the 
context of product life cycles and operational life cycles (Sarkis, 2003). 
Yet, this body of research calls out the need for studying the uniqueness 
of construction supply chains due to the short-term nature of projects, 
varied stakeholders, and challenges in supply-chain communication 
(Badi and Murtagh, 2019). Similarly, circular supply chain management 
is a growing topic of interest for researchers, though it usually focuses on 
automobile and electronics industries but other industries, including 
construction, need additional research (Lahane et al., 2020).
Reverse logistics and reverse supply chains have a sim-ilar focus on 
increasing the recovery of products at their end-of-use. Literature most 
often motivates reverse logistics in construction through decreasing 
environmental impacts including generating less waste, using less raw 
materials, and less greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, while also provid- 
ing some economic and social advantages (Hosseini et al., 2015). 
Methodologies are proposed in research (Wibowo and Grandhi, 2017) 
and in standards (e.g., IEC 62309:2004) to estimate the functionality of 
the product for reuse. An-other approach for reverse logistics considers 
cost, value, duration, and environmental impacts, and demonstrates a 
high return on investment for the recovery of building com-ponents 
(Mollaei et al., 2023). However, these calculations assume available 
information on existing building materi-als, which often is not the case, 
but could be facilitated by information, communications, and 
technology initiatives (Wijewickrama et al., 2021a).
Related strategies include Enterprise Resource Plan-ning (ERP), 
which is a shared software for organizational functions.
